themes.consensus_view: Banks broadly treat the closed Strait of Hormuz as a live oil-supply disruption, and the two desks that take a directional view both read it as a structural shortfall big enough to push oil higher and stoke inflation.

facts_agreed.claim: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz is causing a large oil supply shortfall that is feeding through into broader inflation and growth stress.
evidence_quotes: shortfall of at least 9 mb/d created by the closure
the building blocks of a global stagflationary shock are falling into place

themes.consensus_view: Most banks still believe the huge spending boom on AI computing power is real and will keep pushing big tech earnings higher, but a sizeable minority warns the trade is dangerously crowded and vulnerable to rising interest rates.

facts_agreed.claim: Banks agree that hyperscaler capital spending on AI infrastructure is surging and driving record earnings estimates for chipmakers and big tech.
evidence_quotes: Capex projections have moved sharply higher, driving positive earnings revisions
consensus pointing to 87% EPS growth in 2026, driven by the AI infrastructure buildout
We view compute capacity as a competitive differentiator and increasingly important to the ROIC proposition.

facts_agreed.claim: Banks agree the AI-spending theme remains the dominant force driving the equity market and that demand for compute is still structurally intact.
evidence_quotes: the pillars of this AI cycle are intact
We maintain our conviction in the secular trend of AI
we view them as manageable at this stage and continue to believe that the segment’s structural growth trajectory remains intact
The existential threat has moved away from geopolitics to the fear of missing out on AI.
underlying bid for AI was still prominent

facts_contested.claim: Whether the AI capex super-cycle can keep powering the rally or is a fragile, crowded trade about to break
facts_contested.for_evidence: the strength of the Q1 earnings season combined with the improving long-term outlook for productivity
facts_contested.against_evidence: reflexive flows that fueled the vertical squeeze are now starting to wobble

facts_contested.claim: Whether rising interest rates and bond volatility threaten the capital-intensive AI spending cycle
facts_contested.for_evidence: We maintain our conviction in the secular trend of AI
facts_contested.against_evidence: AI melt-up may finally be running into the one thing investors stopped worrying about: rates.

facts_contested.claim: Whether recent semiconductor weakness signals a regime shift away from AI or just routine profit-taking
facts_contested.for_evidence: not a regime shift away from the AI theme, in our view
facts_contested.against_evidence: semis/AI are likely to ‘catch down’ to the rest of the market

themes.consensus_view: Banks across eleven research desks reference the Iran-US conflict as a live macro backdrop driving oil prices and bond yields, but none has staked a clear directional view on how it resolves.

facts_agreed.claim: Eleven banks reference the Iran-US conflict as an ongoing macro backdrop spanning the risk of war, ceasefire developments, and energy-price impact.
evidence_quotes: Trump canceling planned attack on Iran
US strikes on Iranian military targets

falsifiable_predictions.claim: Full-scale military conflict or sustained closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

themes.consensus_view: Banks broadly agree the market has dropped its earlier bets on Fed rate cuts and is now leaning toward rate hikes, with most desks arguing inflation and the Iran war justify a higher-for-longer stance.

facts_agreed.claim: The market has shifted away from expecting Fed rate cuts and is now pricing in rate hikes.
evidence_quotes: Market participants are increasingly scaling back their previously dovish stance toward the Fed
market has now swung to pricing in Fed rate hikes
bond market is materially more hawkish than our Fed forecast

facts_agreed.claim: Sticky inflation, worsened by the Iran war, is the driver behind fewer expected cuts and higher yields.
evidence_quotes: we now expect fewer or no cuts across the world
Inflation never went away, and the war in Iran has only inflamed it further.
higher rates and firmer inflation apparently here for longer than expected
Investors' calculus in terms of dip buying has changed

facts_contested.claim: whether the hawkish repricing is overdone
facts_contested.for_evidence: bond market is materially more hawkish than our Fed forecast
facts_contested.against_evidence: we now expect fewer or no cuts across the world

themes.consensus_view: Banks across six desks flag a breakout in government bond yields, with the US 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields pushing to multi-year highs, but no desk has staked a clear directional trade on it.

facts_agreed.claim: Multiple banks flag a breakout higher in government bond yields, centered on long-dated US Treasuries, as a live market development.
The US 10-year Treasury yield has climbed to around 4.65-4.67%, roughly 45 basis points above its April lows and the highest level in years.

themes.consensus_view: Banks across six desks reference Kevin Warsh taking over as Fed Chair as a live policy catalyst, but nobody has staked a directional view on what it means for rates yet.

facts_agreed.claim: Six research desks flag Kevin Warsh's appointment as Fed Chair as an upcoming policy catalyst this window.
evidence_quotes: Kevin Warsh confirmed as Fed Chair
Kevin Warsh appointment as Fed Chair
Kevin Warsh Fed chair policy outlook

themes.consensus_view: Banks agree long-term US government bond yields are pushing higher and the market is settling into a 'rates stay high for a while' regime, driven by government borrowing concerns, oil, and rebuilt risk premium.

facts_agreed.claim: Long-end US and global government bond yields are rising and pricing a higher-for-longer rate environment.
evidence_quotes: This environment of flatter curves and higher yields is what my models would classify
pricing is drifting toward a higher-for-longer regime driven by fiscal concerns

themes.consensus_view: Banks across five desks reference US-Iran nuclear deal negotiations as a live macro subject, but none has staked a directional view on the outcome.

facts_agreed.claim: Five banks flag US-Iran nuclear deal negotiations as an ongoing macro development in their notes this window.
